column11: Sotah 5a: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan said: The Hebrew word for person, adam, written: Alef, dalet, mem, is an acronym for efer, dust; dam, blood; and mara, bile, alluding to man’s insignificance. column11: Sanhedrin 57b: ‘It is derived from the phrase “at the hand of every animal” that one is executed even without forewarning, as an animal certainly cannot forewarn someone. It is derived from the phrase “I will require it; and at the hand of man,” with “I” stated in the singular, that the sentence is issued on the basis of the testimony of even one witness. It is derived from the phrase “at the hand of every man,” that the judgment and testimony must be at the hand of a man, but not at the hand of a woman. It is derived from the term “his brother” that the testimony of the witness is accepted even if he is a relative of the defendant.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 20, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 57b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and under Noahide law one is liable to death through a single witness even a relative (Sanhedrin 57b); and in their view he had the status of a pursuer (rodef), and "he who comes to slay you, slay...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For behold, even for fetuses that have not emerged headfirst, an Israelite is not executed for murder; and even for descendants of Noach who are held liable for fetuses, fetuses specifically were included [in Sanhedrin 57b] from the phrase "man in man" (Bereishis 9:6), but wasteful emission is not included in the prohibition of bloodshed, as proven from the words of Tosafos cited above, that its prohibition is rooted solely in the positive commandment of procreation.

column11: Berakhot 33a: ‘The Gemara cites another halakha stating that he must interrupt his prayer in a case of certain danger. column11: Nedarim 65a: ‘GEMARA: The mishna taught that according to Rabbi Meir certain matters are similar to, but in fact do not constitute a new situation, such as a vow which states: Entering this house is konam for me, as there is a bad dog there, where the halakha is that if the dog dies, it is not considered to be a new situation. column11: Sukkah 52b: ‘Rav Ḥana bar Aḥa said that the Sages in the school of Rav say: There are four creations that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created, yet He, as it were, regrets that He created them, as they do more harm than good. column13: As stated in Sukkah (52b): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," which aligns with our principle: capacity to advance matches vulnerability to descend, and lofty stature entails proportionate potential lack; just as immense wealth demands far greater safeguarding than a trivial item, being more susceptible to theft because thieves target it; so too with the soul: the greater its stature and the more divine energy it possesses—and as noted, even the capacity to will the opposite is a divine potency, wherefore man alone, being in the image of God, possesses the drive to rebel—.

column11: Shabbat 77b: ‘On the topic of the nature of the world, the Gemara relates that Rabbi Zeira found Rav Yehuda, who was standing at the entrance of his father-in-law’s house, and observed that he was in an especially cheerful mood. He therefore posed questions to him on a variety of topics unrelated to halakha. He asked: Why do goats walk in front of the flock and then ewes follow? Like the creation of the world, where initially was darkness...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: As in Shabbat (77b): everything created serves a beneficial purpose; and in the Future all will be rectified, no creature perishing: "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb," "and dust shall be the serpent's meat"; and of the nations: "For then will I turn to the peoples a pure language" [Zephaniah 3:9], becoming servants to Israel as explained below; for then Israel will resemble the Holy One, blessed be He, in cosmic symmetry [as in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (ch. 18) on Judges 18:6: "Were it not written it could not be said," as I explained there].

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 2:4: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish interpreted the verses regarding the [four] kingdoms. “The earth was emptiness” – this is the Babylonian kingdom, as it is stated: “I have seen the land, and behold, it was emptiness and disorder” (Jeremiah 4:23). “And disorder [vavohu]” – this is the Median kingdom, [as it is stated:] “They hastened [vayavhilu] to bring Haman” (Esther 6:14). “And darkness”– this is the Greek kingdom, which darkened Israel’s eyes with their edicts, as they used to say to them: ‘Write on the horn of a bull that you have no portion in the God of Israel.’ “Upon the face of the depths” – this is the evil kingdom [Edom], which cannot be calculated, like the depths; just as the depths…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 2:4) to illuminate his exposition here (“and they embody the kelipah of darkness, – as written (in Bereishit Rabbah): "'And darkness' — this is Greece who darkened the eyes of Israel". column13: And the swine displays its split hooves—this is the wicked empire of Rome/Edom: robbing and plundering, while erecting judicial tribunals; clothing its murders in the guise of law and order for the public good. column15: “A man who makes a vow .…” (Bamidbar, 30:3)It is said in the tractate Nedarim (vows) (10a), “what is konam? Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said that it is a term that sages reserved for vows.” This is similar to what is written (Job, 28:28), “The fear of God is wisdom, to turn from evil is understanding.” Wisdom is when one considers everything carefully, understanding with his approval that the action is proper to do, and separating himself from that which is not proper.

column11: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 34: ‘Write thou these words refers to Scripture, and after the tenor of these words alludes to the Mishnah, which was transmitted orally. column13: Rather, because there is no other way to arrive at full understanding, the stumbling itself becomes a preparation for grasping the words of Torah. column13: And the beginning emerges from darkness and mingling among the nations, being "as an apple tree among the forest trees"; and afterward it shines brighter until midday, then being the daytime feast of the Ancient Holy One (Atika Kadisha), which represents that which transcends hidden intellect, concealed from the eye of man himself.

With Yaphet, on the second, and Shem on the third, with whom Noach could speak from the depth of his heart and reveal all his secrets.

column11: Zohar, Tetzaveh 10:83-11:92: ‘Besides, the words of the Torah can best sink into the soul there in the desert, for there is no light except that which issues from darkness, for when that “other side” is subdued the Holy One is exalted in glory. And when a man enters upon an evil way and then forsakes it the Holy One is exalted in glory. column13: Yearning for nothing other than to fulfill the commandments of the Torah; but the yetzer gaining strength through the Serpent's instigation injects sluggishness into the heart from cleaving passionately unto words of Torah; and then automatically when encountering temptation, the heart's inclination which is evil from youth covets selfish gratification; wherefore the initial strike of "the first of the nations" [Amalek] against the Jewish heart operates through this debilitating force!

column15: 80–83: Only after creation endured the devastation of the Flood was this ownership firmly forged with greater power; for the essence of rectification is enabling creatures to receive the light, achieved through additional garments, alluded to in the rectifications of the Idra (Zohar Naso 135b): “to fashion glory for His glory”; and in Zohar (Balak 204b): “The primordial light shone so brilliantly that worlds could not bear it; what did the Holy One do? He fashioned light within His light to enclothe one within the other.”

column11: Shabbat 130a: ‘Apropos affection for the mitzva of circumcision, the Gemara cites a baraita in which it was taught that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Every mitzva that the Jews initially accepted upon themselves with joy, such as circumcision, as it is written: “I rejoice at Your word as one who finds great spoil” (Psalms 119:162), and as the Sages explained, this “word” refers to the mitzva of circumcision, over which they rejoiced, they still perform it with joy. column13: Therefore, in this physical world within the exile that is likened to night (Pesachim 2b), where the subjugation to foreign empires hinders the execution of positive commandments [unlike negative commandments, where one must sacrifice all his wealth to avoid violating them, as codified in Orach Chaim 656 and Yoreh De'ah 157], the mitzvah of tefillin was held laxly in our hands (Shabbat 130a), for the clear awareness of Anochi is not evident to all the nations, existing as it were in a state of concealed countenance.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 4 (§2)
column15: So it was with the tribes when they wanted to kill Yosef; then the basis of the prohibition against killing was hidden from them, and he was only saved from counsel outside the realm of Torah. This also saved his brothers from sin. Yehuda was a great sage in the wisdom of this world, therefore he devised advice and said, “what profit [ma beitsa].” This means, even though that it seemed to him that it was lawfully permitted to kill him, as will be explained, still, what benefit will we receive by killing him?, .

column11: Berakhot 62a: ‘The Gemara asks: Why must one not wipe himself with his right hand, but with his left? A demon (sa'ir) may be confused with a goat (sa'ir)", and Rashi explained: "The demon...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is the 'lesser luminary' and humbleness, which, on the contrary, touches upon the nature of desire as mentioned above, yet through it they conquer lust, just like David who was small and made himself humble, and does not need to conquer lust through its opposite, which is prideful elevation. And it is known that the moon governs the power of the waters, and as the moon waxes the waters increase, unlike the drying sun; for the moon, on the contrary, swells the natural water/desire, and specifically within it lies the rectification.

column15: Akin to what is taught (Mekhilta, Yitro) that no slave could flee from Egypt, because it seemed to him better to serve Egypt than to be a prince elsewhere. column11: Shabbat 152a: ‘The Gemara relates that Rav Kahana was reading biblical verses before Rav. When he got to this verse, Rav sighed. Rav Kahana said: We can derive from this that Rav’s desire has ceased. Rav Kahana also said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “For He spoke and it was, He commanded and it stood” (Psalms 33:9)? He understands this to mean that God created man with desires that push him to do things he would not do if he acted purely on the judgment of his intellect, and Rav Kahana therefore interprets the verse in the following manner: “For He spoke and it was”; this is a woman that a man marries. “He commanded and it stood”; these are the children who one works hard to raise. A…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 152a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as we explained from: "A woman is a vessel full of filth, etc." (Shabbat 152a), and therefore it is called sa'ir.”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Therefore: "The statutes of Hashem are right, rejoicing the heart" [Psalms 19:9], infusing uprightness to purge lusts, as Maimonides wrote (Hilchot Issurei Biah 22:21) that a person is filled with lust only in a heart vacated of Torah; and the Sages taught: "If this repulsive one encounters you"—the lustful inclination (Shabbat 152a)—"drag him to the study hall" (Kiddushin 30b), for the pure desire for Torah entering the heart expels alien, repulsive desires from within it.

column15: So too the drop of life, which descends from the brain, will not bring about birth until it becomes coarse and conglomerates in the seed of man. For at the moment of conception the consciousness of man (before God) is interrupted and forgotten, and if a man’s consciousness could stand constantly before his Creator then he would not be able to experience this concealment and forgetting necessary for conception.Therefore Er, since he only looked towards “bringing honor from his fellow man,” meaning that he always had a clear and brilliant intellect, and stood in the presence of God, therefore he did not want to detract from this.

column11: Kiddushin 72a: ‘The Gemara relates: There was a certain man who said to the Sages: I am from a place called Shot Mishot. column13: And within lust there are three general categories: monetary greed and hoarding wealth—this is the husk of Babylon; the lust for physical indulgence in gluttony and fornication—this is the husk of Persia; and the lust for prestige, dominance, and intellectual arrogance—this is the husk of Greece. And the root of appetite resides in physical indulgence which is Persia's defilement, wherefore their outward guise was modesty in eating and intimacy; modesty simulating restraint, while their inward essence was unbridled lust.

column11: Berakhot 62a: ‘It was taught in a baraita in tractate Derekh Eretz that Rabbi Akiva said: I once entered the bathroom after my teacher Rabbi Yehoshua, and I learned three things from observing his behavior: I learned that one should not defecate while facing east and west, but rather while facing north and south; I learned that one should not uncover himself while standing, but while sitting, in the interest of modesty; and I learned that one should not wipe with his right hand, but with his left. Ben Azzai, a student of Rabbi Akiva, said to him: You were impertinent to your teacher to that extent that you observed that much? He replied: It is Torah, and I must learn.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 62a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And to this allusion they stated (Berachot ibid.): "None is termed modest except one who is modest in the privy", for the title of modesty applies to one who fences himself from lust, as written...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And he was the opposite of Saul, as our Sages taught regarding II Samuel 6:16 "and Michal despised him", complaining that he was not conventionally modest. column13: And it is known that all which Israel gives to the gentile nations derives from the deeds of the Patriarchs in that gift—a sign for the children. column11: Sanhedrin 37a: ‘Reish Lakish says that the source to rely on them not to transgress is from here: “Your temples [rakkatekh] are like a pomegranate split open” (Song of Songs 6:7), which teaches that even the empty people [reikanin] among you are as full of mitzvot as the pomegranate is full of seeds. Rabbi Zeira says that the source is from here: The verse states concerning the occasion when Isaac blessed Jacob: “And he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him, and said: See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). Do not read “his garments [begadav]”; rather, read: His traitors [bogedav], meaning that even traitors and sinners among the…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 37a) to illuminate his exposition here (“which they expounded (Sanhedrin 37a): "Do not read 'his garments' but 'his traitors' (bogdav)", which was the foul odor of washed goatskins; and through this they merit: "and he blessed him", by...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And 'even the empty ones among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate' (Sanhedrin 37a), and as written (there): 'He smelled the fragrance of his garments (begadav)—his betrayers (bogedav).' Nevertheless, there remain distinct spiritual gradations. Prayer essentially signifies connection and cleaving, and this explains why no man is spared from iyun tefillah: for in this, even Jacob's realm is not entirely uniform such that all would be identical and unified without levels in cleaving.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Beshalach 5 (§4)
column15: The power of Moab and its kelipah was strength, strengthening their minds with a healthy diet and the like. Their particular form of idolatry was Chemosh (meaning “dried”), meaning the form of a man dried up from its childhood form. Their fear was that this power would be taken away, like an old, senile man with little appetite.Now God dispersed Israel among the nations so they would be among these powers, to clarify, refine, and clean themselves concerning them, not turning to them but rather placing their trust in God.

column11: Sotah 49a: ‘The Gemara poses a question: But if everything is deteriorating, why does the world continue to exist? The Gemara answers: By the sanctification that is said in the order of prayers, after the passage that begins: And a redeemer shall come to Israel, which includes the recitation and translation of the sanctification said by the angels, and by the response: Let His great name be blessed, etc., which is recited after the study of aggada. As it is stated: “A land of thick darkness, as darkness itself; a land of the shadow of death, without any order” (Job 10:22). Therefore, it can be inferred from this verse that if there are orders of prayer and study, the land shall appear from amidst…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 49a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And it states (Sotah 49a): "Purity cancelled taste and scent, etc., I smell the scent of youth; he said to him: My son, purity is in you." And the true meaning of purity is from defilement issuing...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And likewise Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi], his son, the son of Rabban [Shimon ben] Gamliel, “held fast to humility,” as they said [end of Sotah 49a], “when Rebbi died, humility ceased,”… when Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, the honor of the Torah ceased… and when Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] died, humility and fear of sin ceased [batlah anavah v’yiras chet].” Meforshim: Rashi and the Bartenura — with Rebbi’s death there was none who so embodied humility; and the Gemara (Sotah 49b) relates that when the tanna taught this, Rav Yosef said, “do not teach that humility ceased — for I am here,” and Rav Nachman, “do not teach that fear of sin ceased — for I am here.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 5 (§4)
column15: So why does “you shall not have” not precede Anochi in the order of the mitzvot? In God’s great compassion and understanding our limitations he preceded “Anochi” before, “you shall have no false gods,” for if he had not, no one could ever come to an understanding of the declaration, “Anochi,” for who in the world can say, “I have refined my heart in all the prohibitive mitzvot?”Concerning this, David haMelech said (Tehilim, 138:2), “For You have made Your saying greater than Your name.” “Saying”, as opposed to “speaking,” Dibbur.

column11: Eruvin 21b: ‘Rava interpreted the verse cited above homiletically as follows: What is the meaning of that which is written: “The mandrakes [duda’im] yield a fragrance, and at our doors are all manner of choice fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved” (Song of Songs 7:14)? “The mandrakes [duda’im] yield a fragrance,” these are the young men of Israel who have never tasted the taste of sin.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 21b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as written (Eruvin 21b): – "'The mandrakes give forth a fragrance' — these are the youths of Israel who have not tasted the taste of sin", and on this it specified "youths of Israel", for that...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: The foundational entry of a Jewish child into Torah is establishing this proprietary acquisition, being an inheritance entrusted into their hands completely; and within this verse resides that divine power through which the Torah becomes an acquired possession. As is known that every verse in the Torah contains the living power of that specific reality; just as the mitzvah of the Shema resides in "Hear, O Israel," where declaring it causes his heart to genuinely listen.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Nitzavim 7 (§4)
column15: Then when one comes to the meaning of words of Torah, then “it is not in heaven, and not across the sea … but it is near unto you, in your mouth,” etc. Therefore, Moshe Rabeynu specifically wrote these words in this Parsha, which follows the fiftieth Parsha in the Torah, for then he had attained this level (the fiftieth gate of understanding), that of “it is not in heaven, but near.”This means that even though a man needs fences and boundaries while he does not yet understand words of Torah, once he understands them, he does not need this.

column11: Berakhot 40a: ‘We learned in the mishna: One who recited: Who creates fruit of the tree, over fruits of the earth, did not fulfill his obligation. The Gemara asks: That is obvious, as fruits of the earth do not fall under the rubric of trees. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: This ruling in the mishna is only necessary according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who said in another context that wheat is a type of tree, as we learned in a baraita: The tree from which Adam, the first man, ate, Rabbi Meir says: It was a vine, as nothing brings wailing and trouble upon man even today other than wine, as it is stated with regard to Noah: “And he drank from the wine and became drunk” (Genesis 9:21). Rabbi Neḥemya…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 40a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And for this reason they are termed "figs" based on what is stated (Berachot 40a): – "The tree from which Adam ate was a fig", because intense sweetness is found in them for food, which represents...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is the Two Loaves brought from wheat (Chitah, corresponding to the twenty-two letters of the Torah; wherefore in the Future wheat is destined to soar high like a palm tree, as the Sages stated at the end of Kesubos (111b); unlike now where its celestial light is concealed; and so it was before the Fall, wherefore Rabbi Yehudah holds (Berachos 40a): "the Tree of Knowledge was wheat," it having been a fruit tree; and on Shavuot it returns to the status of a fruit tree.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Shmini 1 (§9)
column15: Since they were young, they were not included together with Moshe and Aharon, as it is said in the holy Zohar (Shemot, 37b), “they did not take their [Moshe and Aharon’s] advice.”What advice did they disregard? One opinion in the Gemara tells us that “they were drunk from wine,” claiming that they came to this state of intense closeness and became, God forbid, irreverent.

column11: Zohar, Noach 9:56-10:63: ‘R. Hiya and R. Judah, while once going on their travels, came to some huge mountains, in the ravines of which they found human bones left over from the generation of the Flood. They measured a bone and found to their amazement that it was three hundred paces long. They said: ‘This bears out what our colleagues have said, that the men of the time of the Flood did not fear the vengeance of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, “They said unto God, Depart from us, for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways” (Job 21, 14), and that one of the things they did was to stop up with their feet the fountains of the deep, until the waters which bubbled up became too hot for them to endure,…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Noach 9:56-10:63) to illuminate his exposition here (“This initial assumption was based on what is stated in the Zohar (Part I, 62a and elsewhere) regarding this blemish that its repentance is exceptionally arduous; because this is contingent upon...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: However, in the Holy Zohar [Vayechi 219b] we learned, Rabbi Yehudah said: "We have no sin in the world for which there is no repentance except for this one"; behold, this minimizes the power of this sin as if repentance does not avail for it at all! And the early masters already cried out over this, for behold nothing stands in the way of repentance; and in Parashas Noach [62a]: "All sins of man depend upon repentance, but the sin of spilling seed... 'your iniquity is marked before Me' (Yirmeyah 2:22), except through abundant repentance," thus far.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:3 (§2)
column15: Just as a pitchfork turns over the grain, etc., so does the prayer of the righteous turn the disposition of the Holy One from strictness to compassion.” And as brought in the holy Zohar (Tazria 46a): “'And man became a living soul'—into a speaking spirit capable of speaking before the King.” And all desires and needs of creatures are subsumed in the power of prayer, and every person should ensure that prayer reside at the root of his soul, so that he does not desire what is contrary to Hashem's will, being an agent of free choice.

column11: Sanhedrin 93b: ‘Rabbi Alexandri says that the term hariḥo teaches that God burdened the Messiah with mitzvot and afflictions like millstones [reiḥayim]. Rava says that hariḥo teaches that the Messiah will smell [demoraḥ] and then judge on that basis, sensing who is right, as it is written: “And he shall neither judge after the sight of [lemareh] his eyes, nor decide after the hearing of his ears; and with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and decide equity for the meek of the earth” (Isaiah 11:3–4).’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 93b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And then the Messiah will "judge by scent" (Sanhedrin 93b), where the sense of pure holy fragrance will be perfected, as stated of him: "And his smelling shall be in the fear of Hashem". – And on...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And the infallible verification of perception in Wisdom will be realized in Mashiach, concerning whom they stated in truth that he is exalted above Moshe Rabbeinu (Tanchuma, Toldos 14); and "he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither decide after the hearing of his ears" (Yeshayah 11:3) from witnesses, but rather "he smells and judges" (Sanhedrin 93b); and scent is that from which the soul derives pleasure, as they stated [in Berachos 43b]; and this corresponds to the verse "the breath of life in his nostrils" (Bereishis 2:7).
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 41:7
column15: And in the days of the Messiah when Israel conquers the seven nations in wholeness, then the harp will possess eight strings (Arachin 13b), and the eighth string will not be a brand-new entity, rather the seven strings will be clarified, and Hashem will radiate His light within them to illuminate them in clarity, shining before all eyes that Israel has conquered the seven nations in perfection; and then divine justice dictates that the three nations beyond their self-refinement will also be granted them.

column11: Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 22:21: ‘Similarly, a person should distance himself from levity, intoxication, and flirtation, 25:1) and Chelkat Mechokek 25:1. for they are great precipitators and steps [leading] to forbidden relations.A man should not live without a wife, for this practice leads to great purity. And [our Sages gave] even greater [advice], saying: 30b. "A person should always turn himself and his thoughts to the words of the Torah and expand his knowledge in wisdom, for the thoughts of forbidden relations grow strong solely in a heart which is empty of wisdom." And in [Solomon's words of] wisdom [Proverbs 5:19], it is written: "It 54b which explains the analogy in detail. is a beloved hind, arousing favor. Her…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 22:21) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as stated in the Rambam of blessed memory (end of the Laws of Forbidden Relations): "The thought of illicit relations overpowers only a heart vacant of wisdom." And through Torah study he will...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: While Wisdom is the absolute antidote to all lusts, which are termed folly (Sotah 3a: "A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him"), and as Maimonides wrote (Hilchot Issurei Biah 22:21) that one should direct his heart to words of wisdom, which rescue from worldly lusts, the Torah being "a lovely hind and a graceful doe" [Proverbs 5:19]; see there.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Beshalach 2 (§5)
column15: There is no greater nonsense.“If there is no wisdom then there is no fear,” refers to one who has no trust in God, yet he is constantly in a state of fear even without the inspiration from the Torah, then his fear is not authentic but rather imaginary, as one who truly fears God has tekifut in his heart and trust in God.

column11: Avodah Zarah 19a: ‘The Gemara relates: Levi and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, were sitting before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and they were learning the Torah portion. When they finished the book that they were learning and were ready to begin a new subject, Levi said: Let them bring us the book of Proverbs; and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, said: Let them bring us the book of Psalms. He compelled Levi to acquiesce, and they brought a book of Psalms. When they arrived here, at the verse: “But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord,” Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explained the verse and said: A person can learn Torah only from a place in the Torah that his heart desires. Levi said: My teacher, you…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 19a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And the word yirah (awe) points to repentance, – as they expounded (Avodah Zarah 19a): "'Happy is the man who fears Hashem' — happy is he who repents while still a virile man"; and so they said...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And as stated (Avodah Zarah 19a): initially the Torah is called by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, but ultimately it is called by the scholar's own name, as it is said: "But his delight is in the Torah of Hashem, and in his Torah does he meditate day and night" [Psalms 1:2]; meaning ultimately, when he becomes a great master with the halakhic authority to complete, adjust, restrict, and enact enactments in words of Torah, it is called his Torah, being the fruit of his labor.

column15: “Speak to the children of Israel … a man or woman who commits any of the sins that men commit ….” (Bamidbar, 5:6)The sin mentioned is stealing from a convert who dies before compensating him for the loss (see Rashi on Bamidbar 5:8). Here it appears that teshuva (repentance) is of no use., 219b) writes, “Rabbi Yehuda said, there is no sin in the world for which there is no teshuva (repentance) to rectify it except for this, and and there is no evil one who cannot see the face of the Shechina except for one who does this, as it is written (Yeshaya, 60:21), “and Your people are all righteous .…” Although there is nothing man can do from his side, God can surely rectify it.

column13: And this explains: "and from my disciples more than from all of them" (Ta'anit 7a), for a person has primarily one master (Avodah Zarah 19a); and even if he has more, colleagues are far more numerous, and disciples most numerous of all without end, and he absorbs the Torah insights within each disciple that he lacked, learning more from them through their sheer number.

column15: It seems that it may be explained through the verse (Tehilim, 145:14), “God supports all those who fall, and straightens all those who are bent down.” Two things are mentioned in this verse—fallen, and bent down.This means, with one who has anger and evil lusts rooted in his heart, if God forbid he brings his potential into action, it is called “fallen.” If it still has not been brought forth into action, he is called “bent down,” meaning that his heart is bent and enslaved to this evil lust.

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rava was wont to say: The objective of Torah wisdom is to achieve repentance and good deeds; that one should not read the Torah and study mishna and become arrogant and spurn his father and his mother and his teacher and one who is greater than he in wisdom or in the number of students who study before him, as it is stated: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them” (Psalms 111:10). It is not stated simply: All who fulfill, but rather: All who fulfill them, those who perform these actions as they ought to be performed, meaning those who do such deeds for their own sake, for the sake of the deeds themselves, not those who do them not for…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and so they said (Berachot 17a): "The purpose of wisdom is repentance, etc., as said: 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem'"; and through Torah study one possesses always the power to...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column13: For from the nature of the afflictions one can always discern the targeted purpose intended by them, for they are ever meted out measure for measure, as it is said (Isaiah 27:8): "In full measure, when You sent her away, did You contend with her". And the subjugation to foreign empires mirrors the yeast in the dough [the Evil Inclination], as stated in the second chapter of Berakhot (17a): just as the Evil Inclination seeks the literal reverse of the good—as it is said (Isaiah 5:20): "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil"—so the subjugation of empires desires the exact opposite of the ultimate divine objective.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:4
column15: “Your people offer themselves willingly in the day of your power” (Psalms 110:3)— meaning that the entire world will willingly desire and volunteer to submit beneath the spiritual attribute and devotions of Avraham our Father, since he is inseparably bound to Hashem, blessed be He, constantly. “In the beauties of holiness”— meaning that he rectified all actions of preceding generations that were performed in a deluge of willful sin and a torrent of wickedness.

column11: Proverbs 4:22: ‘They are life to those who find them,Healing for the whole body.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Proverbs 4:22) to illuminate his exposition here (“as Scripture states: "healing to all his flesh" (explained often); and it is written: "The fear of Hashem is pure, enduring forever", which refers to the Torah (Zohar Part III, 80b), which stands...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And will generates thought, focusing his thoughts on this alone. And this is what they expounded (Eruvin 54b): "'they are life unto those that find them'—unto those who articulate them with the mouth," for words of Torah are termed a "tree of life," the letter Vav of the divine Name traversing from end to end: passing through all parts of the soul within his body—brain, heart, and limbs of action—it is called a tree of life.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1 (§2)
column15: This will necessitate that they have true fear, and this is the explanation of “those who fear My name.” promising them that He will shine the sun of tsedaka upon them, or in other words, refined words of Torah. “Of healing in her wings” means trust, or taking strength in God and in words of Torah, just as wings are the trust and strength of the bird.We find that before God was revealed to him, Avraham Avinu derived no satisfaction from all the matters of this world, and even despised them.

Jose: ‘But it says here “the fear of the Lord”, and not “the Torah”?’ He replied: ‘It means the same thing, because the Torah comes from the side of Geburah (Might).’ Said R. Jose: ‘Rather derive it from here: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ibid. 111, 10). It is written: “The fear of the Lord is pure”,’’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 21, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Kedoshim 1:6-3:13) to illuminate his exposition here (“and it is written: "The fear of Hashem is pure, enduring forever", which refers to the Torah (Zohar Part III, 80b), which stands eternally for a person to cleanse him and purify his soul so that...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Whereas King Solomon, peace be upon him— embodied the attribute of Malchut (Sovereignty), the feminine aspect and the spiritual organ of the mouth, and we designate this “the Oral Torah”, as stated in the discourse of Patach Eliyahu, because it is the fresh, innovative insight arising continuously within the hearts of Knesset Yisrael.

column11: Pesikta Rabbati 6:2: “On the twenty-fifth of Kislev the work of the Tabernacle was completed, yet it remained folded and waited for three months until the first of Nisan, when Moses erected it on the day Isaac was born. Kislev therefore felt deprived, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘It is incumbent upon Me to repay Kislev,’ and He repaid it with the dedication of the Hasmoneans on the twenty-fifth of Kislev.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 22, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Pesikta Rabbati 6:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“And it states in the Pesikta (Parashah 6): that the Tabernacle was completed on the 25th of Kislev and stood folded until the 1st of Nisan, etc.; did Kislev lose out, etc.? What did the Holy One...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And it appears that this is what R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon said [Bava Metzia 83b], “rejoice, my innards!” — for when it was clarified that there is in him no sin of bloodshed, through this a holy one can dwell within his innards, and all his eating is like korbanos, from which his fat and flesh were formed. And we learned [in the fifth chapter of Avos, and Yoma 39a] that “the holy flesh never became putrid” — all the more the flesh of the holy man, whose innards are in the place of the altar, and the growth of whose flesh is from holy eating that is like a korban, to which no putrefaction pertains at all.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 19:1 (§2)
column15: However, over those who trust in Hashem, He supervises with individual providence, as brought in the holy Zohar (Vayeira 103b): “'Her husband is known in the gates'—this is the Holy One, blessed be He, Who is known and attached according to what one measures in his heart, etc.”; meaning: for the sake of one trusting in Hashem, He watches over the entire world with individual providence, akin to what is brought in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit Rabbah 39:12): even barrels of libation wine being transported from Gaul to Spain.

column11: Bava Batra 115b: ‘Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai recited this verse about him: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan and Shobal and Zibeon and Anah” (Genesis 36:20), and it is written: “And these are the children of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah” (Genesis 36:24). The first verse portrays Zibeon and Anah as brothers, while the second states that they are father and son. Rather, this teaches that Zibeon engaged in sexual intercourse with his mother and begot Anah, so that he was both Anah’s father and his brother. From the fact that the first verse equates Zibeon and Anah by referring to both of them as Seir’s sons despite Anah being a grandson of Seir, it is clear that grandchildren…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 115b) to illuminate his exposition here (“for the Twelve Tribes constitute the collective of Knesset Yisrael, as written (Bava Batra 115b): "It is a tradition that a tribe never ceases". While the dedication of the Hasmoneans was from the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For at that singular instant he stands at the head of cosmic governance, and this operates individually in each distinct moment. And in general, Israel is divided into twelve tribes, each of which represents a distinct, autonomous character; see Horayot (5b), and they are so permanently fixed and established that it is impossible for them to be altered, just as they taught (Bava Batra 115b): 'it is received as tradition that a tribe is never utterly eradicated'.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 2 (§3)
column15: At first, when his father and mother conceive him, he is completely hidden, unrecognizable to any part of creation. The second state of being occurs when he is formed in his mother’s womb and becomes recognizable as a separate entity. The third, when he is born and his existence is complete.

column13: The explanation of this is as stated (Nedarim 35b): "These Kohanim are the emissaries of the Merciful One," dedicated to serving His holy service, blessed be His Name, and therefore he is termed "a messenger of Hashem of hosts," for they were set apart and designated exclusively for this, as it is said (Deuteronomy 17:9): "And you shall come unto the priests the Levites," (II Chronicles 15:3): "without a teaching priest," and ibid. chapter 17 concerning Jehoshaphat appointing judges, and in other places, for they were uniquely consecrated to teach the Torah of Hashem.

column15: This is because the entire need for speech is only in order to communicate with others, as by himself he has no need for speech. The Torah exists in all of the worlds, so above this world “do not steal” means not to prevent the Torah from reaching one’s students (Sanhedrin, 91b).

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 98: ‘“Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of villainy are their heritage” (Genesis 49:5) “Simeon and Levi are brothers” – brothers of Dina but not brothers of Joseph. “Weapons of villainy are their heritage [mekheroteihem]” – he said to them: These weapons in your possession have been stolen by you. For whom are they fitting? column11: Berakhot 5b: ‘The Gemara returns to the topic of prayer. column13: When a person walks from bright light into slight darkness, he cannot see initially; but if he remains there for some time, he begins to see. Therefore, when a person is born he lacks mature discernment until he grows up. And one who abides continuously in slight darkness acclimates and sees well therein; and this explains why one who studied and then abandoned the path is harsher than an ordinary ignorant person Pesachim 49b, for "a mitzvah is a candle, and the Torah is light" Proverbs 6:23, and our Sages stated Sotah 21a that the Torah is likened to a great blazing torch.

column11: Sotah 21a: ‘The Gemara asks: Does the merit of a mitzva protect one so much as to delay her punishment? column11: Mishnah Maaser Sheni 5:15: “Yochanan the High Priest did away with the confession of the tithes. He also abolished the ‘wakers’ (me’orerin) and the ‘strikers’ (nokfin). Until his days the hammer used to strike in Jerusalem on the intermediate days of the festival; and in his days no man needed to inquire concerning demai (produce about which there was a doubt whether it had been tithed).” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 24, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Mishnah Maaser Sheni 5:15) to illuminate his exposition here (“And behold we find (end of Chapter 5 of Ma'aser Sheni) enactments from Yochanan the High Priest, and the Bartenura explained that he served after Shimon the Righteous, and so wrote the Rambam...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: A mitzvah performed on account of doubt certainly bears the holiness of the Blessed Name, since fulfilling it out of doubt is an established obligation, exemplified by the second festival day of the Diaspora (Yom Tov Sheni). And see Shabbat 23a that we recite the blessing "Who has sanctified us with His commandments" even over matters of doubt, with the exception of demai (doubtfully tithed produce) because the majority of common folk do tithe see my halakhic novellae on this.

column13: Therefore it is taught in Gittin (57a): Balaam's punishment in Gehinnom is in boiling semen, for this was his essential root and destructive power. And as written in Zohar Balak (194b) regarding what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said to the Queen of Sheba, see the explanation there. The explanation being as written on 193b: Balaam in defilement stood as the counterpart of Moses our teacher in holiness, and just as Moses our teacher is the root of all wisdom of all the sages of Israel throughout all generations (Shabbat 101b: "Moses, you have spoken well"), so Balaam is the root of all wisdom of all the sages of the nations throughout all generations.

column11: Gittin 57a: ‘§ It was stated earlier that the city of Beitar was destroyed on account of a shaft from a carriage. The Gemara explains that it was customary in Beitar that when a boy was born they would plant a cedar tree and when a girl was born they would plant a cypress [tornita]. And when they would later marry each other they would cut down these trees and construct a wedding canopy for them with their branches. One day the emperor’s daughter passed by there and the shaft of the carriage in which she was riding broke. Her attendants chopped down a cedar from among those trees and brought it to her. Owing to the importance that they attached to their custom, the residents of Beitar came and fell…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 24, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 57a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written (Gittin 57a): "and they kindled lamps until the seal of a signet ring could be seen a mile away"; and so we find in Midrash Rabbah (Eichah 4:100): "The child fell silent on Chanukah,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column15: Every king has two attendants, one a wine steward and the other a baker. Truly, with the wine steward, if the king finds a fly in his cup it is not proper to punish him, for what could he do? The fly is an independent living creature, and if once the cup has been passed to the king the fly decides to land into the cup, then it is not possible to guard from it.

column15: And behold, the power of reproduction generated in the human form, and especially in the birth of a male child, is channeled from the influx of the Name Havayah; and from this is born a creature capable of expanding and generating further on its own; and therefore, since procreation issuing from the male force derives from the essential light of Hashem, it is impossible for birth to occur except through forgetfulness and concealment, entirely beyond human conscious intellect, purely from the essential light and power of Hashem.
